title: Shvetaketu comes home
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: a boy comes home after twelve years of study, proud and missing one thing
carry: vidya: learning that frees, not learning that puffs up
tomorrow: can a king with a crown teach a monk about freedom?

lines: AWAY AT TWELVE. HOME AT TWENTY-FOUR.
DID YOU ASK FOR THE ONE TEACHING?
cards: A boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Vedas. He comes back at twenty-four, and the Chandogya Upanishad, telling his story, doesn't flatter him: conceited, thinking himself learned, stiff with it.

His father, Uddalaka, lets him settle in. Then he asks one question. Did you ask your teachers for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known?
Twelve years of study, and Shvetaketu has to say: no. What is that teaching?

teach.b: Hold that boy in mind and read Isha nine. Andham tamah pravishanti ye avidyam upasate: into blind darkness go those who worship not-knowing. Fair.
Then: into greater darkness, as it were, go those who delight in knowing alone. That's Shvetaketu at twenty-four. Two small words keep it from being an attack on learning.

teach.h: IVA: A PICTURE, NOT A VERDICT.
teach.b: Iva, as it were: a picture, not a verdict. And ratah, delighting in, as if learning were the whole point. Verse ten adds iti shushruma dhiranam: thus we have heard from the wise.
Shushruma comes from the same root as shruti, the Hindu name for the Vedas themselves: what is heard, passed from teacher to student. Now the debate. What do vidya and avidya mean here?
Shankara reads avidya as ritual works and vidya as worship of the gods; each alone falls short.

teach.h: AUROBINDO: THE ONE AND THE MANY.
teach.b: Sri Aurobindo hears vidya as knowing the One and avidya as knowing the many, and says a full life needs both. They disagree on the pair. They agree on the warning: learning that only puffs you up is its own kind of dark.

The Mundaka Upanishad even calls study of the Vedas the lower knowing, and the knowing of the Imperishable the higher. And this is the tradition that sets its books before Saraswati to be blessed. It loves learning.
It just asks what the learning is for.

how: Students of the Isha usually read verses nine to eleven with a commentary; on Saraswati Puja many families place books and instruments before the goddess of learning to be blessed.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: reading the Isha's own words, small ones like iva included
reading the Isha as a warning to stop studying
reading the Isha's rules for which books to avoid

games.q: the proud student and the verse — tap the pairs.
p: as it were: a picture, not a verdict

s: Isha 9 says plainly that learning leads into darkness
iva, as it were: it warns against delighting in knowing alone, like Shvetaketu.
shushruma, 'we have heard', shares a root with shruti, the name for the Vedas
shruti: what is heard, passed teacher to student.
Shankara and Aurobindo agree on what vidya means here
Shankara reads worship of the gods; Aurobindo, knowing the One. both warn against one-sidedness.

games.q: your study partner reads vidya and avidya as knowing the One and knowing the world. you're asked to give Shankara's case at its best. what is it?
o: the verse is against learning of every kind, full stop.
rites alone or worship alone both fall short; freedom needs more than either.
the verse is about school, and it says to study less.
games.why: Shankara reads avidya as ritual works and vidya as worship of the gods. each alone falls short; the verse warns against one-sidedness, not learning.

practice: Vedanta names three steps of study: shravana, hearing; manana, thinking it over; nididhyasana, taking it to heart. Today, just the first. Listen the way a student once listened to the wise: no notes, no answers.
Let one sound at a time come and go, near and far, without naming it. If you pray, say Om once, softly, and listen to it fade.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, verses nine and ten: iva, as it were, and iti shushruma, thus we have heard. A warning, not against learning, but against learning alone.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: shruti, what is heard, the Hindu name for the Vedas, from the same root as shushruma.

carryVoice: Your line: vidya, learning that frees, not learning that puffs up. Shvetaketu found out at twenty-four. Until the next verse.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 9, first line (andham tamah pravishanti ye 'vidyam upasate)
sources.q: andham tamah pravishanti ye avidyam upasate

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 10 (anyad evahur vidyaya anyad ahur avidyaya; iti shushruma dhiranam ye nas tad vicacakshire)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–3 (Shvetaketu leaves at twelve, returns at twenty-four, conceited; Uddalaka asks about the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard)
Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.4–5 (two knowings: the lower, including the four Vedas; the higher, by which the Imperishable is grasped)
Shankara, commentary on Isha Upanishad 9–11 (avidya as karma, ritual works; vidya as knowledge and worship of deities)
Sri Aurobindo, Isha Upanishad commentary (vidya and avidya as knowledge of unity and of multiplicity)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (the self is to be heard, reflected on and meditated on: shrotavyo mantavyo nididhyasitavyah; the basis of shravana, manana, nididhyasana)
